More horrific, is the fact that Science is being carried out to please the PI's ego or a skewed vision of facts lending to publications of either cherry-picked data not entirely reflecting the complete scenario or simply 're-inventing the wheel'. Q26.text: It's a mixed bag—some great mentors and collaborative vibes, but also a lot of pressure, bureaucracy, and uncertainty about career paths.
Q26.original_text: I have an extremely low opinion of the academic system after my PhD experience. I was excited to work in an environment where creativity and new ideas were appreciated and I could learn new things all the time. I expected that I would work hard and long hours, but not so hard that I burnt myself out. However, looking back now, I absolutely wouldn't do this again, and I wish I had quit during my qualifying exams like I wanted to, but I was talked out of it. Sexual harassment and bullying are so pervasive that at this point I am surprised when my peers haven't experienced it. Expectations are consistently unreasonable and students completely burn themselves out trying to meet them and receive little to no recognition when they do. Stipends are so low that many graduate students struggle to make ends meet, to the point where many experience food insecurity. Professors receive little to no training on management, mentoring, or teaching, which causes harm to students when do all of these jobs poorly. Funding is extremely inequitably distributed, with "big name" labs and a handful of "prestigious" universities getting a huge amount of the funding, and other labs doing valuable work struggle to get a single grant. Also, basic research projects trying to generate new knowledge, which are supposed to be the lifeblood of academia, are almost never funded. To be funded now, research apparently has to have immediately realizable applications.  There is no diversity of thought among faculty, as the only people who can actually become faculty now all come from the same few universities, and in many cases even from the same advisors. People who struggle with their mental health during graduate school are often driven out rather than helped. Teaching loads are often unreasonable and don't even teach valuable skills, but simply take up graduate students' time. Universities use bureaucracy as a way to keep from making changes, and it is easier for them to just wait out student complaints until they graduate rather than address them. Graduate programs are not actually set up for graduate students to learn, as the "degree" would lead you to think - it is set up to use graduate students as a source of cheap labor to generate research and revenue for the university. In turn, the university barely acknowledges graduate students, focusing their energy and resources on undergraduate students and faculty. Diversity is not valued, and people from diverse backgrounds are much more likely to quit at every stage because the environment is untenable for them.

Q26.text: Ate o momento, consigo  perceber que fazer um Doutorado em um pais com uma cultura extremamente diferente e que e automaticamente refletida na cultura educacional, e um desafio tremendo, que tem impacto direto na saude mental dos estudantes. Por exemplo, venho da cultura ocidental, onde hierarquias quase sao nulas (as relacoes sao bem horizontais); a autonomia, a proatividade e a liberdade no ambiente academica sao consideradas como qualidade e bem vistas pelos Professores; o equilibrio entre vida pessoal e profissional tambem sao bem vistos e devem co-existir. Entretanto, no Japao, a sociedade e extremamente hierarquizada e essa hierarquia e refletida fortemente no ambiente academico, onde os professores sao tomam uma posicao enorme de poder e respeito, colocando-os em uma posicao inacessivel ao estudante. E isso abre tambem precedentes gravissimos para a quase institucionalizacao do abuso moral e de poder (e, uma vez, que a hierarquia e sumariamente respeitada, esses episodios quase nao sao reportados por parte dos estudantes). Ainda, considerando esse posicionamento dos professores nessa hierarquia engessada, os estudantes nao sao bem vistos se questionam, apresentam personalidade e demandam discussao (a relacao e sempre muito de submissao e negacao de discussoes). E, por ultimo, o Japao e reconhecido como o lugar que as longas jornadas de trabalho 12-14 horas por dia sao bem vistas (nao import se isso leva a uma produtividade ou nao, se a pessoa esta sofrendo ou nao), o status valorizado aqui e quantas horas voce se mantem no ambiente de trabalho e anule a sua vida pessoal. Desse modo, a ciencia aqui, que demanda debate, discussao, opinioes e completamente negada pelo sistema hierarquico, bem como sao valorizados os estudantes que vao se degradando fisicamente ao longo do seu Doutorado. Adicionalmente, o Japao e um pais, extremamente xenofobico e, enquanto estudante internacional, esse preconceito e sentido em cada detalhe da vida academica, onde, nao importa o que voce faca, atinja ou demonstre: no final e cada esquina, voce sera sumariamente desacreditado, descredibilizado e desencorajado. E, toda essa situacao nao se aplica a mim, se estende a todos os outros estudantes internacionais que aqui convivo. E algo realmente muito grave e dificil de mudar.

Q26.text: First of all, in the Netherlands, bright people are leaving academia due to the lack of grants. It is very hard to pursue an academic career when you stay in the Netherlands. Therefore, I moved to the USA to follow working in academia as a postdoctoral researcher, and I hope that this experience will give me (some) advantage in grant applications when I move back to the Netherlands in 3-4 year.   Secondly, although i started working as a postdoctoral researcher here in the USA, I am still finishing my PhD program, due to the Dutch system. As molecular cell biologists, we need to have 2 published papers and a third submitted to a peer-reviewed journal, before you can finish your thesis and set a date for a defense. Since publishing has become harder over the years (more data needed, extensive peer-review cycles that are both very consuming when the manuscript is rejected after review and needs to be submitted elsewhere where the whole cycle will start again), I have not been able to finish my PhD in the time set to do so. I started as a PhD-student in August 2013 and was supposed to finish in 4 years. Then, I was extended with one year and I left for a postdoc in Augstus 2018. To date, June 2019, I'm still not finished since manuscript acceptance takes too long.   I was lucky that my new PI here in the USA was understanding that defense in the Netherlands depends on publications, but officially I am not working as a postdoc now, but as a research specialist on a postdoc project. I know of a lot of Dutch colleagues that had to let go of their dream of a postdoc in the USA, because of this problem.  I think it is unfavorable that PhD programs differ so much between countries. I think the Dutch system aims for a very high standard, which I like, but it diminishes opportunities to succeed later in your academic life.

Secondly, although i started working as a postdoctoral researcher here in the USA, I am still finishing my PhD program, due to the Dutch system. As molecular cell biologists, we need to have 2 published papers and a third submitted to a peer-reviewed journal, before you can finish your thesis and set a date for a defense. Since publishing has become harder over the years (more data needed, extensive peer-review cycles that are both very consuming when the manuscript is rejected after review and needs to be submitted elsewhere where the whole cycle will start again), I have not been able to finish my PhD in the time set to do so. I started as a PhD-student in August 2013 and was supposed to finish in 4 years. Then, I was extended with one year and I left for a postdoc in Augstus 2018. To date, June 2019, I'm still not finished since manuscript acceptance takes too long.   I was lucky that my new PI here in the USA was understanding that defense in the Netherlands depends on publications, but officially I am not working as a postdoc now, but as a research specialist on a postdoc project. I know of a lot of Dutch colleagues that had to let go of their dream of a postdoc in the USA, because of this problem.  I think it is unfavorable that PhD programs differ so much between countries. I think the Dutch system aims for a very high standard, which I like, but it diminishes opportunities to succeed later in your academic life.

Q26.original_text: I went into an area I didn't have very much previous experience in, molecular biology. I did this willingly, and my supervisor was well aware of this, but I was under the impression that the teaching would be more supportive than it has been. As such, catching up has been a much greater struggle than I felt it had to be, and this has changed my view of academia, and myself. Overall, I had the feeling that has been repeated by others when I've talked to them about this: beginner level information on a topic is usually freely available, but doesn't go into enough detail. Expert level information on a topic can usually be located, but is typically too dense to comprehend, particularly within the time-frame that you need to understand it. What you might call intermediate level information is usually lacking; you need most of the detail you would find in something aimed at experts but explained in a way that a beginner might have a shot at understanding readily. I have a degree in biomedical sciences, so I had some prior knolwedge of molecular biology. As such I found myself in the "intermediate" stage with too large a knowledge gap I needed to close in seemingly too short a time. I was expected to do end-point experiments within a week of starting that no one else had managed to make work, and with virtually no prior experience in the necessary tissue culture. My supervisor suggested I might have results in a fortnight. There were few relevant books I could get hold of - most were too simple anyway. There were few lectures available to go to, and although I tried to gain access to undergraduate and masters material in relevant areas, it took a long time before this access was granted, and even then, some of what would have been highly relevant was missing. You need a lot of valuable information to be very readily available if time frames are going to be that short and you are lacking prior experience. I do not feel, from communication with other graduate students, that I am particularly alone in this experience. It has been a struggle to get anyone to explain things in plain English, and frequently embarrassing to try. I have been told things like "I know this too well to explain it to you simply", which I personaly think is ridiculous but seems to be a generally accepted attitude in academica. Academic journals are no help in this department. While I appreciate the need for specialist terms in science, the more I eventually do understand, the more it appears that most of the language in journals is often pretty unneccessarily complicated. Sentences that could just be straight forward, even those that need specialist terms, are typically anything but. This makes comprehension that much harder. It feels like elaborate blocks of text are there more for trying to maintain an aura of academia, and sometimes to persuade the reader of your view whether the evidence supports it well or not, rather than getting the information into another person's head. Given that graduate students, that can't really be seen as experts, will often be reading these journals (and given how often I have heard or read graduate students complaining about how hard journals are to read), it seems strange that the information can't be geared towards this group, especially considering that using plain langauge shouldn't confuse more expert readers. I appreciate that there are almost countless specialist fields with an extremely large volume of knowledge that is constantly changing and therefore almost impossible to organise. However, I get the feeling that politics and preserving and dealing with people's egos takes up more of my time than understanding what has gone before and what I have to do now. This experience has, of course, made me severely doubt my own intelligence and abilities., but I can't help thinking that it must be possible to explain most things very clearly, so if it isn't explained clearly and simply, there must be a reason why people don't want to.

Q26.text: The academic system is designed to train PhD students to become PIs. In the process of doing so, PhD students gain valuable experience and transferable skills that make them competent and resourceful individuals. However, the expectation is very much that you would continue on to a post-doc position. This, in my view, is not a good thing given the relatively few academic jobs available. PhD programmes should establish closer links to industry and and other non-research related science careers to ensure that PhD students gain the skills aligned with these careers after they graduate, and build networks to facilitate job opportunities. PhD programmes and institutions also do not articulate well enough the capabilities of PhD graduates to employers in the wider sector, and can improve on this.  PIs and funding bodies have a lot of incentive to employ PhD students and post-docs in the short term on temporary contracts, but the academic system should incentivise instead the hiring of permanent staff scientists for those who want to be in the lab full-time. For those that don't, greater exposure to other career paths (eg. talks, networking opportunities, work experience placements and internships) is needed for PhD students' career progression.  In many cases, poor supervision from the PI and a negative group environment can detract from the PhD experience - this is really hard to judge from a short interview.

Q26.text: This system is designed to break people slowly, so they don't realize what's happening until we can't sleep through the night and we feel guilt for watching tv on the weekends just to have a small break. Most of the grad students here are living in unhealthy situations. I am currently living in a house with termites and roaches 10 miles away from campus because it's all I can afford. My advisor quit her job as a professor and left me with no funding for my final semester of grad school, plus she has been a poor advisor overall because she is consistently underprepared, late, or distracted. I do not feel like a priority to her. Moreover, as an early career researcher herself, she doesn't have much experience or knowledge of opportunities even within academia, much less outside of it. I have been neglected for YEARS now, and no one can do anything about it because this kind of over-committed workload is considered "normal." Everyone is subjected to it, and it's expected of pre-tenured faculty. If this is all I have to look forward to, why would I want to stay in academia? I'm seriously rethinking my life goals. I don't want the rest of my life to be scrounging for money and working 60 hours a week with no chance of a break. The PhD has made me hate academia and question myself on every level, especially when it comes to the value of a PhD. I feel like I wasted my time earning one just to be thrown into a post-doc hell where the pay isn't much better and I'm still ignored. I want to do work that matters and has an impact. I don't think academia has that anymore, at least not from my perspective.

Q26.original_text: During my 7 years veterinary medical training in China, I got used to the “Chinese” schedule. We came to work at 8 AM and left around 10 PM, often working on the weekends. Not much time for a social life or hobbies, so you made your job your hobby and your co-workers your social life. But here, I was amazed that everyone comes to work at 9 AM and  leaves at 5 PM. And forget about working on the weekend.  Because they don’t stay for those long hours like in China, I thought they don’t work hard enough. Later on I realized that I am actually the one who is not working hard. Staying in the lab/office longer than the others does not means I work harder. The other PhDs are all 100% focused on their work during the eight-hour working period and super organized, while I was taking so called “breaks (facebooking/instagramming/messing around here or there a bit)” . I struggled with my inefficient and poorly planned long working hours at the beginning, but finally resolved to change.  I don’t have to follow their working schedule, but I found that it is much more efficient, I am more engaged, and  I get to have a life after work for the first time.

Q26.text: The academic system needs a drastic overhaul. It has become a corrupt and abusive system. I would like to see major reforms at every single level. Most research is published for the sole reason of publishing a paper. Papers and impact factors have become the currency of academia; the desire to do Science for the sake of progress or humanity is largely non-existent. Most places and people care about the length of the CV, but no thought is spared towards the impact these studies may have had. Further, the Ph.D. student is left at the mercy of the supervisor and the academic system which tends to protect itself when questioned. Universities have become brands and they care too much about their brands. Harassment cases are quietly stamped out to protect the university's and the supervisor's reputation. This is true more so for international students who put their entire careers and lives on the line to work towards their Ph.D.s on a pittance. Lip service is paid to women empowerment, but women are consistently left out at every possible turn. A strong teaching effort is drummed up by universities, but everyone knows teaching takes away from one's ability to manufacture papers. It looks incredibly bleak for academia unless one is well-connected and comes with the right brand and backing. The way I see it, academia has stagnated and it does not look like things are changing for the better any time soon. Of course, one can write an entire article, and many have been written without much effect, about the publication system and the exorbitant cost of acquiring "knowledge" in today's world.

Q16.text: I find it absolutely baffling that academia, while propped up as the last bastion of ethical and moral purity, tolerates faculty and students with alarming behavioral issues. In my experience, I have seen faculty members get away with sexual harassment and abuse at multiple universities with supreme confidence. Further, the biggest lesson I have received during my Ph.D. is that academia rarely cares about merit or quality. There are, to the best of my knowledge, only two ways to get ahead: my advisor is well connected and/or I somehow manage to find my way onto a Nature or Science publication. Maybe this is to be expected given the shortage of jobs, but it makes academia an ideal breeding ground for abusive relationships. I also find that enough is not done to make incoming students understand how slim the chances of an academic career really are, post Ph.D. Maybe it is too much, and not even the point of a Ph.D., to train students for careers outside of academia. However, the system is nothing short of a scam if incoming students are, at the very least, not made aware of the reality of the job market. Precious few universities and departments actively expose their students to opportunities outside of academia by encouraging participation in workshops, conventions, presentations, alumni networks, etc. And no, it is not the sole responsibility of the incoming student to know how the job market is. It is similar to arguing that sweatshops employing immigrants in the Middle Eastern countries carry none of the blame and arguing instead that the blame must rest on the people working there "voluntarily".  And make no mistake, academia today is eerily similar to a sweatshop.

Q16.original_text: I am volunteering at a peer support group and what concerns me the most is the poor mental health of students and the lack of resources to support students. In my center students are doing PhD for an average of 6 years (there are cases that students have been in their PhD for 8 years) and the mental state is below average (students are crying in the student room and are having nervous break downs almost every week. You can imagine how working in such an environment feels for the rest). Abusive PIs do not get punished for their actions and there is not proper HR for students that are facing difficulties. At my university the order to deal with a certain issue is to: 1. Talk to your supervisor, 2: talk to the program director, 3: talk to your thesis committee, 4: talk to the university. I am not sure how comfortable students are discussing about project related issues with any of the previously mentioned authorities since none of them can really do anything. Another issue that I think has a huge impact is that fact that there are a lot of PIs that are hiring their spouses as research assistants or close relatives for summer interns. I have the feeling that they are using public funds to run their laboratory as a family business while it is not. I feel that there is no organizational justice.

The obligation in our country to have at least one first author paper in a peer-reviewed journal is too burdensome and very often impossible within the standard study length. In some fields of study, such as experimental biology, meaningful research takes quite a long time and when the student is new to the field, it takes about 2 years just to learn the methods and theory. Under the conditions that we have, we are either forced to publish low-quality articles or to extend our studies, which is very stressful and often considered by society and academic representatives as a failure. Q60.text: Yes! I entered my dissertation program focusing on research that bridges two different fields. In the beginning of my program, I was revered for that smart, forward-thinking twist to my research, and I was told repeatedly this is where the field needs to go (inter-disciplinary). Now, I am struggling to finish my dissertation, because every topic I suggest for my dissertation has been rejected by everyone in the department, since it is not traditionally within my field. And I never wanted this to happen to me, I had three options (I knew they were feasible, because another graduate student I worked with previously swiped one of those topics and graduated early and with praise) for dissertation topics as I entered the PhD program, because I knew I didn't want to be like other students I saw in my department that just appeared to take funding opportunities away from everyone while not progressing to graduation. Now I am that student. I even had a NSF DDIG proposal ready to submit (edits from the department lasted over 5 months, and it was ready!), and I was told they day of submission to our Office of Research, I should not submit, because no one in the department could supervise the project. I have since seen students AND professors independently come across those topics I have been steered away from, and those topics have been funded by major federal institutions, and the research yielded multiple publications in noteworthy journals. I am doing a dissertation project now that was not my idea, I have been handed the data, and it is my job just to analyze data that no one has used since the 1980's, just so I can graduate in 6 years. I know I sound like a complainer who is blaming everyone else for my problems. Maybe that is the case. I am saddened, because with those rejected topics have also gone my rose-colored glasses about the ability of research in academia to allow you to pursue passion projects. And even though my department publicly touts inter-disciplinary projects, there is no support for that in my department. It clearly took me too long for that to sink in.   Overall, I wish I had a mentor explain those hard facts to me; I wish I was smart enough to read between the lines to see inter-disciplinary research is not what my department produces; and I wish it did not have to be that way. Now, I just hope to graduate (later than I intended and with a project I am not sure contributes to modern society in any way), find an academic job (seemingly a one-in-a-million chance), and work to support inter-disciplinary research every day of my life.

Q26.text: Academic system is very bureaucratic and professors spend too much time in teaching and administrative duties. Since I like doing research, this discouraged me to pursue a professorship. There is a lack of full-time/tenured researchers who can provide solid advice on research methods and practice. Professors mostly don't do research themselves, besides quickly reviewing papers or thesis. This was a huge disappointment for me, because I thought I would have a strong and deep mentorship on research practice in the university setting.  The publish-or \-perish mentality is also a waste of the little time professors and postdocs have. This mentality makes people push for half-backed research results  (or hyped buzzwords) in order to increase publication count (or be present at a conference). The result (in my field at least) is a flood of low quality papers that are 90% written by students. This low quality takes enormous time from reviewers and makes conferences boring as participants barely ask questions or discuss the topics. Instead, I feel that most people are mostly interested in seeing and being seen.

Q60.text: When the survey questions uses the term "programme", it makes me assume that there should be a structure in the PhD graduate studies. I don't believe there is a structure, and I am not sure that it is possible or desirable to have one. Graduate school is not like the undergraduate school. While the undergrad school looks like a production of line of professionals, the graduate school experience is more of a one-to-one coaching. Therefore, "programme" could be a misleading term. I would not like to be in a strict standardized PhD program. I would rather have access to senior researchers who would actively advise me in various topics.   Now, we face the worst of the two worlds. US PhD programs are littered with artificial barriers, e.g., required lectures, required exams, required publications, required teaching assistant practice, etc). Meanwhile, these programs do not provide access to senior researchers (only to busy professors who don't practice research themselves because they are overloaded with lectures and administrative duties).   I think the survey should have also explored the topic of conferences and workshops. Conferences and workshops are sometimes advocated as events for students to get feedback. However, they are overcrowded, professors are busy meeting other professors, and people barely ask questions after the talks. The exception was the Doctoral Symposiums, where PhD Students get feedback on their research from a panel o professors. This was a great experience that I have in more than one conference.  The survey could have addressed bullying more deeply. As a graduate student, I saw the bullying of colleagues as the most serious issue in the university that I attended (UC Irvine). I would like to see more awareness and discussion about that. Is bullying cultural? Or is it a consequence of excessive competition in the US academic system?

Q26.text: I think the academic system is really powerful to develop professionally and personally. It is full of challenges that make you grow in all possible aspects. One can develope his/her own expertises over the years and built on them to participate in different projects and ideas. As a PhD student I can really see that I know much more now than when I started my degree (same way at that moment I knew more than before starting my Master's degree). The academic system is also very unique in the sense that it provides a multicultural environment where it is possible to meet and exchange ideas with people that come from all over the world. This leads to the formation of a very powerful scientific community. However, there are two things that I believe create a lot of issuess in the academic system as it is now. First, as I mentioned before, the only way to continue being in the system is by publishing and, of course, the higher the impact factor of the journal, the higher the chances to be successful and continue in academia. However, there are other factors apart from pure Science that affect a publication or the generation of the data and I think there should be a way to consider them. Second, there are very few (almost none) regulations on how to be a group leader. Even if PIs do get evaluated by the amount of publications that their group produce, nobody checks how they are treating their people and how they actually do Science. Once the position of group leader is reached, there is almost complete anarchy to do everything. This means that if you end up in a good group your possibilities to stay in the academic system will definetely improve. However, if you are in a group where the work environment/conditions are not the best, then it is highly likely that you don't want to do Science anymore after your PhD. And sadly, this is the reality of what is currently happening in academia and the amount of PhD students that want to pursue a career is dangerously decreasing because there is a high rate of group leaders that do not treat their people correctly.

Q26.original_text: El sistema académico (por lo menos en España) se ha visto gravemente mermado en los últimos años por los recortes en inversión en educación e investigación por parte de partidos neoliberales, que tienen como objetivo último la privatización de no sólo el sistema académico, sinó también el sistema médico, pensiones, etc. Debido a la gravedad de la situación, las condiciones laborales dentro de la universidad se han visto muy afectadas, apostando por un modelo que busca trabajadores que deban renovar sus contratos anualmente, en vez de plazas de lector y plazas fijas, cobrando los primeros un sueldo mísero que muchas veces no cubre ni la mitad de la manutención mensual, forzando al pluriempléo del profesorado. Los que ahora estamos cursando nuestros PhD lo tenemos peor, porqué se nos fuerza a dar clases a los no graduados, muchas veces de asignaturas troncales, sin ningún tipo de remuneración y durante las horas que se deberían invertir en el PhD. Ello no sólo nos lastra a nosotros, sinó que implica que el sistema académico (en este caso la universidad) se ahorra mucho dinero dejando de contratar a profesorado para dar esas clases gracias a la docencia gratuita que los PhD son obligados a dar. Para hacer una comparativa, a un compañero que está haciendo el PhD en Dublín le pagan las horas de docencia a razón de 17 Euros/hora. Yo soy uno de los que menos horas de docencia ha dado en mi departamento este año, pero de todos modos, si se aplicase lo mismo debería haber cobrado unos 450 euros (26 horas de docencia).

This all trickles down to students, who are either forbidden from presenting research, asking for information from other labs that are experts in a certain area in order to get useful information or sent on a wild goose chase without any means of actually getting somewhere. The pettiness is also prevalent within the same department of the university, where a certain PI dislikes another and this gets placed on the students, creating an awkward and unfriendly atmosphere that is entirely counter-productive.

The idea that it is not the quality of research, but the 'attractiveness' of the answer at the point of (attempted) publication, that ultimately defines the future success of PhD students is abhorrent. The disproportionate focus on publications over other qualities, particularly at ECR stages, when competing for the very limited number of academic jobs is a terrible way of determining competence. Even after a postdoc/fellowship has been secured there is an almost immediate need to begin searching for the next position, which, in many cases leads to a significant investment in time that could be used for research. The prospect of battle for job-rinse-repeat, often for greater than a decade before securing a permanent post (which is by no means guaranteed) is driving the more capable students, with more prospects external to academia, out of the place they are needed most (i.e. education) and into the arms of industry.

Q26.original_text: The academic system is mainly based on the assumption that you will continue with an academic career path once completing your PhD course. In my experience there is little guidance and support for those who have decided not to pursue that pathway.   The emphasis placed on publishing as many papers as possible, and the use of this as an indication of your research capability and work ethic creates a stressful environment where working excessively long hours is celebrated and encouraged. The "publish or perish" mentality has been the major challenge I have faced within the academic system as some areas/ disciplines in research are more time consuming than others, and thus the typical three year time period of a PhD program may allow some to publish numerous papers while others will be limited to a few, if any.       On the other hand, the academic environment allows for collaboration and I have found there is generally good working relationships between academic staff (although I acknowledge that my experience of this is only limited to two university environments). I have also found that there is an increasing emphasis placed on ensuring mental health within the academic system and there is growing support for PhD and graduate students. The freedom to investigate novel and/or fundamental areas of research within the academic system is exciting and allows one to learn/practice creative problem solving techniques which is unique to the academic environment.

Q26.text: The academic system that we follow was set up with the right ethos. But in the execution we have all collectively faltered. It was one field of work which accommodated heterogeneity and diversity in all forms especially ideas and way of life but increasingly the system is trying to homogenize people making them loose their individuality. In older studies, journals reviewed and argued the science behind what the authors did, but now they review and make authors add more experiments which they want to see not necessarily needed for proving what the authors did. If big data is the current trend every research group is expected to have omics in their paper.  There is also this wave of applied research which as a standalone field is very good but inadvertently penetrates into basic research. All research cannot be applied immediately. Lots of drugs that are there in the market exist because their mechanism of action was a phenomenon some graduate student/post doc uncovered which could eventually get targeted. The original study may not even have proposed it. This also encourages researchers to portray hypothetical forced biomedical applications of their research findings and mislead people  when actually there may be none.  I also feel the system inherently assumes that people in academia don't have a life beyond work. They reinforce this assumption in their expectations from students and PIs. In fact its almost considered unusual if you are single and want to leave for home at decent hours after work. Family is the qualifier you need to enjoy time after work. This notion is largely in India. There are other inherent assumptions too like people doing science should look shabby and unkempt. This portrayal of scientists has become like a norm and if you don't fit into their mold you are not considered a serious scientist. People who are well dressed, especially women therefore have a hard time being taken seriously.

Q55.original_text: I now know the value of early and thorough planning in a research project with a results-oriented approach.  Experiments should be well thought out at the earliest stages, starting with a clear research question and then adopting a results-oriented, 'working backwards' approach. This approach to project planning provides the initial direction of the research hypothesis, and then ensures that the research question will be addressed by establishing the type of data needed to address the research question and subsequently planning out appropriate results analysis. Working backwards, the researcher may then plan the experiment based on appropriate power calculations, available time and the project budget. By applying this level of scrutiny to every experiment undertaken within a research project, many unintended or unforeseen errors can be avoided at later stages.

I feel that people pick the wrong reasons to enter the academic system beyond undergraduate, such as prestige, university life and academic "independence". Q26.text: Garbage. While I've been lucky to have an excellent mentor and dedicated committee, the department and school I'm in offer at best little support for graduate students, and at worst, active attempts to sabotage those students. The default assumption is that a funded graduate student will teach all five years of their funding package, and the burden of responsibility of those teaching assignments has steadily increased over the five years of my PhD. For example, introductory lab teaching responsibilities have increased from 2 courses/week per TA to 3 courses/week per TA. This adds another 30 students' worth of grading to grading responsibilities, and another 5 hours per week between actual lab run time (3 hours), setup and cleanup (1 hour) and office hours (1 hour per lab session). This makes it impossible to confine teaching responsibilities to the 20 hours/week we're paid for (if you're spending 15 hours a week teaching, that leaves 5 hours a week to grade 90 lab reports. You try grading 90 lab reports in 5 hours. It doesn't happen--and that's not counting troubleshooting via email or addressing student concerns over email). Additionally, the number of trainings for teaching responsibilities we are expected to complete rises steadily every year, creating an unpredictable time commitment that varies from semester to semester. The end result is a burdensome, difficult to navigate system that means for most of the time you're working, you're doing teaching-related activities. Late in the programme, as I am, this can be deadly--you're faced with a choice of whether to assume debt for your last year or years or quit the programme due to simply not having time for research due to teaching responsibilities.  This wouldn't be so bad if those assignments were predictable and reliable, but they aren't. Colleagues haven't received their contract or their funding until well after the semester's actually started; I've been badgered for weeks by the financial services offices on campus because my tuition remission hasn't gone through in a timely manner. The actual wages do not reflect the cost of living. I am lucky because I receive a degree of financial support from my family, but medical and other kinds of debt among graduate students at my institution is common. I've been cycled through five separate teaching assignments before the semester started, with the administrators responsible indicating that I might not have one, even if my funding package guarantees it. Overall, it means there's a great deal of insecurity in funding even well into the programme and with a funding package.   There is no ability to unionize or organize for better working conditions. This university is in a right-to-work state, and the graduate student government, while claiming to be lobbying for better wages, is in effect toothless and has had no success in improving working conditions. With the expected ruling that graduate student workers are students first and workers second, there is little likelihood that this will change.

Q60.text: Please do something to change the culture around graduate school. We are used as disposable workers, with little support or assistance available, and power imbalances mean that if a faculty member wants you out, you're out. Mental health initiatives are laughable; seeing a therapist once a week treats symptoms, but the underlying cause is an unhealthy, exploitative environment in which students are entirely at the mercy of faculty and paid extremely poorly. It would be better to allocate that money to paying students better and improving working conditions, thus alleviating the prevalent economic anxiety  and mental illness from stress and overwork. Mental health support is a band-aid. It's better to have it than nothing at all, but it doesn't actually prevent the injury in the first place.
